programs.nl_rule:
In the input, you should see...a grid with scattered colored cells.

The output grid size...is the input grid size scaled up by 2 (e.g 10x10 becomes 20x20)

To make the output, you have to...read the input as a grid of 2x2 blocks (a 10x10 input is a 5x5 arrangement of them). Each colored cell sits at an odd row and odd column, that is, in the bottom-right corner of its own 2x2 block, and no block holds more than one. Every block that holds a colored cell becomes a solid 4x4 box of that color at the same block position in the output; every other block is black.

content.text:
The rule: input grid, colored cells at odd rows and odd cols. Output is upscale of downscaled-by-2 grid by 4. Let me think.

Actually simplest: output is the input grid where each colored cell at (odd,odd) becomes a 4x4 box. Equivalent: downscale by 2 gives a grid where each cell (i,j) of downscaled takes input[i*2,j*2]... wait careful.

Let me just think: downscale(I, 2) takes rows where i%2==0 and cols where j%2==0. rot180 twice = identity. So x1 = downscale(I,2) = grid of entries at even indices. Then upscale by 4.

So the output is: take input at even rows and even cols (i=0,2,4,... and j=0,2,4,...), giving a (H/2 x W/2) grid, then each cell scaled to 4x4.

Hmm, but the rule says colored cells sit at odd rows and odd cols. Wait but the example: row 3 col 9 has 3 (odd,odd). Row 5 col 3 = 8 (odd,odd). Row 7 col 5=1. Row 9 col 1=8, row9 col7=2. All odd,odd. So even-index sampling would miss them! But downscale takes i%factor==0 i.e. even. Hmm.

Wait, downscale of rot180(I). rot180 reverses. Let's recompute. rot180(I) puts input cell (i,j) at (H-1-i, W-1-j). Then downscale takes even indices of the rotated. So it takes original indices where H-1-i is even, i.e., i ≡ H-1 mod 2. H=10, so H-1=9 odd, so i odd. Similarly j odd (W=10). Good, so it samples odd rows/cols. Then rot180 again on downscaled. Then upscale by 4.

So output is essentially input sampled at odd rows/cols, upscaled 4x. The rot180 twice just handles orientation but final result is same block arrangement? Let's verify: downscaled grid D has D[a][b] = I[2a+1][2b+1]? Let's check: rot180: (i,j)->(9-i,9-j). downscale picks rows r even: 9-i even => i odd. row index a = r/2, r=9-i, a=(9-i)/2. For i=1, a=4. Then rot180 of D: D[4][b]. Hmm D has 5 rows. rot180 reverses D, so new index 4 -> 0.

Let's just trace example: input cell (9,1)=8. It appears at output as 8 block at rows 16-19, cols 0-3. Block position (4,0) in 5x5. Indeed 16-19 = block row 4. So block row = (i-1)/2 = (9-1)/2=4. Good.

So the mapping simply: block at (a,b) where a=(i-1)/2, b=(j-1)/2, gets color of cell at (2a+1, 2b+1). The rot180 cancels. So output block (a,b) = upscale of I sampled at odd,odd.

Great. So the transform: for each 2x2 block, if bottom-right cell colored, output 4x4 box of that color, else black. Output size 2*input size.

Actually the key risk: student might get the reflection wrong (rot180). The teacher example includes left-column cells so reflection matters. The rule: it's downscale of rot180 then rot180 of downscale then upscale by 4. Let me verify: rot180(I) flips both. downscale by 2 takes every other row/col. Since colored cells at odd rows/cols, in rot180 they're at... Let me just trust the teacher example.

The rule effectively: output block at position (i,j) is color at input cell... The verifier: output = upscale(rot180(downscale(rot180(I), 2)), 4). Let's figure the net mapping. Input 10x10, colored cells at odd row r and odd col c. rot180: cell (r,c) -> (9-r, 9-c), both even. downscale takes rows/cols at even indices: downscaled[i][j] = rot180grid[2i][2j] = I[9-2i][9-2j]. So downscaled grid (5x5) at (i,j) = I[9-2i][9-2j]. rot180 of that 5x5: (i,j) -> (4-i, 4-j), value = I[9-2(4-i)][9-2(4-j)] = I[1+2i][1+2j]. So downscaled2[i][j] = I[2i+1][2j+1]. Then upscale by 4: output block (i,j) becomes 4x4 solid. So essentially each input cell at odd row 2i+1, odd col 2j+1 maps to output block at position (i,j) in block grid, i.e., output rows 4i..4i+3, cols 4j..4j+3.

So it's a straight block upscale, no reflection. Good. The natural language matches. Student should get it.

Now let me show a 12x12 example to show size variation.
